article.title: Building Scalable AI Systems: Lessons from Production
article.subtitle: What we learned deploying machine learning models at scale — and the mistakes that cost us month

paragraphs: When we first started building our AI platform, we thought the hard part was training the model. We were wrong. The hard part is everything that happens after you type model.fit() — deployment, monitoring, scaling, and keeping the whole thing running when real users start sending real data.

This post shares the lessons we learned over 18 months of building and scaling our ML infrastructure. Some of these lessons cost us weeks of debugging. Others cost us months of rework. All of them changed how we think about building AI systems.

challenge.heading: The Challenge
paragraphs: Our platform processes over 2 million requests per day. Each request needs to be classified, routed to the appropriate model, and responded to within 200ms. The models themselves are updated weekly, and we need zero-downtime deployments.

architecture.heading: Our Architecture
paragraphs: We settled on a microservices architecture with a dedicated model serving layer. Each model runs in its own container with autoscaling based on request volume and latency metrics.
The key insight was separating the model serving layer from the business logic layer. This let us update models independently and roll back without affecting the rest of the system.

mistakes.heading: Mistakes We Made
mistakes.intro: We made plenty of mistakes along the way. Here are the three that hurt the most:
mistakes.quote: We spent three months optimizing model accuracy by 0.3%, only to discover that our data pipeline was silently dropping 5% of incoming requests.

items.label: Ignoring data quality.
items.text: We focused on model architecture when the real problem was data quality. Garbage in, garbage out applies more than ever at scale.

items.label: No feature store.
items.text: Without a centralized feature store, different teams computed the same features differently. This caused subtle bugs that were nearly impossible to track down.

items.label: Testing in production.
items.text: We didn't invest in a proper staging environment early enough. By the time we did, we had already shipped several bugs to users.

results.heading: Results
paragraphs: After implementing these changes, we saw dramatic improvements across the board. Model deployment time dropped from 4 hours to 15 minutes. Incident response time fell by 60%. And most importantly, model accuracy improved by 12% — not from better algorithms, but from better data.

takeaways.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Invest in data quality before model complexity
Build observability from day one — you can't fix what you can't see
Separate model serving from business logic
Test with real data in a staging environment
